deep.reconstruction:
This folio is a fair copy of part of a manuscript in which Ramanujan collects q-series identities. He describes the coefficients they give as cases where 'the partition method gives the actual value'. That phrase almost certainly means the Hardy–Ramanujan circle method: the singular series gives the representation number exactly, with no error term. The previous folio has the same S-formulas numbered (1.81)–(1.84) and the T-formulas (1.91)–(1.92), which shows the material was renumbered between drafts. No derivations are written on this page; it is a list of results.

Notation (standard Ramanujan): phi(x) = sum_{n in Z} x^{n^2}, psi(x) = sum_{n>=0} x^{n(n+1)/2}, and chi(n) = chi_{-4}(n) (the nontrivial character mod 4) or chi_{-3}(n) (the nontrivial character mod 3), as indicated.

(3.12) phi^4(x) = 1 + 8 sum_{n>=1} n x^n/(1+(-x)^n). Equivalently r_4(n) = 8 sum_{d|n, 4∤d} d. This is Jacobi's four-square theorem.

(3.13) phi^6(x) = 1 - 4 sum_{k>=0} (-1)^k (2k+1)^2 x^{2k+1}/(1-x^{2k+1}) + 16 sum_{n>=1} n^2 x^n/(1+x^{2n}). Equivalently r_6(n) = 16 sum_{d|n} chi_{-4}(n/d) d^2 - 4 sum_{d|n} chi_{-4}(d) d^2 (Jacobi).

(3.14) phi^8(x) = 1 + 16 sum_{n>=1} n^3 x^n/(1-(-x)^n). Equivalently r_8(n) = 16 (-1)^n sum_{d|n} (-1)^d d^3 (Jacobi).

(3.21) Put t = x^{1/4}. Then t psi^2(t^4) = sum_{k>=0} (-1)^k t^{2k+1}/(1-t^{2(2k+1)}).
- Expanding, the right side equals sum_{N odd} (sum_{d|N} chi_{-4}(d)) t^N.
- For N ≡ 3 (mod 4) the inner sum vanishes. For N = 4n+1 it is d_1(4n+1) - d_3(4n+1).
- So the identity says the number of representations of n as a sum of two triangular numbers is d_1(4n+1) - d_3(4n+1).

(3.22) x^{1/2} psi^4(x) = sum_{k>=0} (2k+1) x^{(2k+1)/2}/(1-x^{2k+1}). Equivalently psi^4(x) = sum (2k+1) x^k/(1-x^{2k+1}), i.e. t_4(n) = sigma(2n+1) (Legendre).

(3.23) With t = x^{1/4}:
16 t^3 psi^6(t^4) = sum_{k} (2k+1)^2 t^{2k+1}/(1+t^{2(2k+1)}) - sum_k (-1)^k (2k+1)^2 t^{2k+1}/(1-t^{2(2k+1)}).
Equivalently t_6(n) = (1/8) sum_{d|4n+3} chi_{-4}(d') d^2 with d' = (4n+3)/d. This follows because the chi_{-4}(d) d^2 sum is the negative of the chi(N/d) d^2 sum when N ≡ 3 (mod 4).

(3.24) x psi^8(x) = sum_{n>=1} n^3 x^n/(1-x^{2n}). Equivalently t_8(n) = sum_{d|n+1, (n+1)/d odd} d^3 (Legendre/Jacobi).

Text: these are 'well known formulae' for sums of 2, 4, 6, 8 squares or triangular numbers. The partition (circle) method also gives exact values in other problems, and he will 'quote a few examples and reserve the discussion to another paper'.

(3.31) S = sum_{mu,nu in Z} x^{mu^2+mu nu+nu^2} = 1 + 6 sum_{n>=1} chi_{-3}(n) x^n/(1-x^n). The signs follow +1, -1, +1, -1 on n = 1, 2, 4, 5. This is the Borweins' cubic theta function a(q); equivalently r(n) = 6 (d_{1,3}(n) - d_{2,3}(n)).

(3.32) S^2 = 1 + 12 sum_{3∤n} n x^n/(1-x^n). The coefficient of x^N is 12 (sigma(N) - 3 sigma(N/3)). Equivalently S^2 = (3P(x^3) - P(x))/2, where P = 1 - 24 sum sigma(n) x^n.

(3.33) S^3 = 1 - 9 sum_n chi_{-3}(n) n^2 x^n/(1-x^n) + 27 sum_n n^2 x^n/(1+x^n+x^{2n}).
- Since x^n/(1+x^n+x^{2n}) = sum_m chi_{-3}(m) x^{nm}, the coefficient of x^N is -9 sum_{d|N} chi_{-3}(d) d^2 + 27 sum_{d|N} chi_{-3}(N/d) d^2.
- This is the weight-3 Eisenstein series with character chi_{-3}.

(3.34) S^4 = 1 + 24 sum n^3 x^n/(1-x^n) + 8 sum (3n)^3 x^{3n}/(1-x^{3n}). The coefficient of x^N is 24 sigma_3(N) + 216 sigma_3(N/3), the weight-4 Eisenstein series on Gamma_0(3).

My own spot checks of initial coefficients all agree:
- S^3: x^1: 18 = -9 + 27; x^2: 108 = 27 + 81.
- S^4: x^1: 24; x^2: 216 = 24·9; x^3: 888 = 24·28 + 216.
- phi^6: x^2: 60 = -4 + 64.
- phi^8: x^2: 112 = -16 + 128.
- psi^6: t^7 coefficient (48 + 48)/16 = 6.
- psi^8: x^3 coefficient 28 = C(8,2).

The point of the page: in these classical cases, and for the forms x^2+xy+y^2 (and x^2+xy+2y^2 on the next page), the generating function's power is a pure Eisenstein series, with no cusp-form part. That is why the circle-method singular series reproduces the coefficients exactly.
errors: No mathematical errors found; every identity checks against initial coefficients.

The series are given only by initial terms with '+ ...'. The general sign and character patterns must be inferred: chi_{-3} in (3.31) and (3.33), and (-1)^n-type signs in (3.12) and (3.14). The inferred patterns are the correct ones.
Nothing is proved on the page; the claim that the 'partition method' gives these exactly is asserted, not justified here.

psi^2, psi^4, psi^6, psi^8 as Lambert series (sums of 2, 4, 6, 8 triangular numbers)
results.modern_name: Legendre/Jacobi formulas for sums of triangular numbers
results.usually_credited_to: Legendre, Jacobi; also in Ramanujan's notebooks Ch. 17 (Berndt Part III)

results.what: S = sum x^{m^2+mn+n^2} = 1 + 6 sum chi_{-3}(n) x^n/(1-x^n)
results.modern_name: Lambert series for the Borweins' cubic theta function a(q); representations by x^2+xy+y^2
results.usually_credited_to: Lorenz (1871); Dirichlet class-number theory; rediscovered by J.M. & P.B. Borwein (1991)

results.what: S^2, S^3, S^4 as Eisenstein (Lambert) series of level 3
results.modern_name: a(q)^k = Eisenstein series on Gamma_0(3) (weight 2, weight 3 with chi_{-3}, weight 4); exactness of the singular series for x^2+xy+y^2 in 2, 3, 4 copies
results.usually_credited_to: Classical modular-forms theory; explicit cubic forms popularized by Borwein–Borwein–Garvan (1994); identities also in Ramanujan's notebooks/lost notebook (Berndt)

results.what: Remark that the partition (circle) method gives exact values for such problems
results.modern_name: Exactness of the singular series (Hardy–Littlewood–Ramanujan) when the theta power has no cusp-form component
results.usually_credited_to: Ramanujan (1918, 'On certain trigonometrical sums') and Hardy (1918–1920) for sums of squares s <= 8; Mordell for further cases

deep.surprise_reason: All identities are classical (Jacobi, Legendre, Lorenz) or appear elsewhere in Ramanujan's notebooks and lost notebook; he himself calls the first group 'well known'. The mildly notable feature is the explicit plan to treat the forms x^2+xy+y^2 and x^2+xy+2y^2 via the circle method as exact cases, an unpublished extension of his 1918 sums-of-squares work. That is a small but genuine historical detail, not a new result.
